extracted.intended_audience: mathematics students and readers interested in proof methodology and Lakatosian philosophy of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Methods for analysing and adapting mathematical proofs when counter-examples ("monsters") appear; compares monster-barring, exception-barring, monster-adjustment, and lemma incorporation and explains Lakatos's preferred practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of monster-barring deals with occurring incompleteness of a proof found through a counter-example by excluding the counter-example explicitly in the definition of an object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define prime numbers not only as 'numbers which are only divisible by 1 and itself', but also explicitly excluding 1 so unique prime factorisation (up to ordering) holds. Note and warning: simply excluding the monster by fiat (e.g. banning 1) avoids the counter-example but may not yield further understanding; however, in some contexts (after algebraic study) such exclusions become natural (±1 are the only units of Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monster-adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: A related method which, after a monster appeared, reinterprets or rephrases the former definition so that the monster 'isn't a real monster any more' and claims the definition was always intended in that way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: count zeros of a polynomial with multiplicity to keep the fundamental theorem of algebra true. This preserves the original statement by changing interpretation rather than excluding cases; it can be seen as retroactive clarification of intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception-barring
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave the conjecture as it is and claim it is still true, but for some (explicitly mentioned) exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: common among earlier mathematicians (e.g., Lagrange stated theorems in maximal generality then immediately mentioned exceptions). Anti-pattern: this approach can ignore what the counter-example teaches about underlying structure and thus limits learning from the failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of lemma incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse at which sublemma the theorem really went wrong and aim to adjust only this lemma; by fixing the problematic lemma the monster is also excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefit: yields additional information about properties of the counter-example by investigating which lemmas must change. Normative guidance: prefer local, targeted changes to lemmas rather than global exclusions; this can preserve other lemmas for more general use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lakatos' preferred criterion: prefer lemma incorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lakatos prefers the method of lemma incorporation over exception- or monster-barring and gives reasons: lemma incorporation leads to learning and genuine theory-improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments given: (1) 'we do not learn anything when applying exception- or monster-barring' because counter-examples are not taken seriously; (2) lemma incorporation forces careful consideration of the counter-example and reveals properties to be noted; (3) adjusting only necessary lemmas advances mathematics since other lemmas may remain true and useful in more general cases (example: Euler's theorem about polyhedra evolving into a theorem in topology); (4) because more counter-examples may exist, conservative/targeted adjustment is preferable. Metaphor: mathematics is likened to science—build a consistent theory and work with it until experiments (counter-examples) force revision—so lemma incorporation is 'good' mathematical practice analogous to good scientific practice.
